clue.text: Chance of money in S Africa to order

blocks.note: the rand is the South African currency
OM is the Order of Merit

explanation.surface: A gamble on South African cash, arranged to someone's order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To order' reads like 'made to order', but order is just the honour abbreviation OM.
explanation.definitionFit: Chance used as an adjective, as in a chance meeting, describes something happening without plan or method, which is random.

clue.text: Inconsiderate style of riding

blocks.note: surface reading: a careless, rude way of sitting a horse
setter's reading: the idiom for trampling over other people's feelings, named after horseshoes with projecting nails

explanation.walkthrough: To ride ____ over someone is to treat them with no regard; the word first described a horse shod with nail heads sticking out for grip.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'ride roughshod over' means to act with arrogant disregard for others, so the word names that heedless manner of riding.

clue.text: A pretty bunch up before the beak

definitions.text: A pretty bunch up before the beak

blocks.clueFragment: A pretty bunch up before the beak
blocks.note: surface reading: an attractive gang of criminals appearing in front of a magistrate

blocks.clueFragment: A pretty bunch up before the beak
blocks.note: setter's reading: a posy of flowers held up in front of the nose, beak being slang for nose

explanation.surface: A fine crowd of villains up in front of the magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: Beak is British slang for a magistrate, and 'up before the beak' means in court; here the beak is a nose, and the small bunch of flowers is held to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small bouquet of sweet-smelling flowers, traditionally carried to hold to the nose, is a pretty bunch.

clue.text: Frequently concerned with decimal multiplication

blocks.note: of can mean about or concerning, as in tales of the sea
multiplying by ten is the decimal step

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps returning to sums involving decimals.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adverb meaning often or many times, a straightforward synonym for frequently.

clue.text: Fellow-volume to old Hawker's miscellany

blocks.note: a chap is a man or fellow
a volume is a book

explanation.surface: A companion volume to an old collection by someone named Hawker.
explanation.walkthrough: Hawker looks like a surname because of its capital; it is a pedlar, the chapman who sold these cheap booklets door to door.
explanation.definitionFit: Small cheap pamphlets of ballads, tales and tracts were sold by travelling pedlars, so it is a hawker's collection of assorted pieces.

clue.text: Past records of Disraeli's supporters?

blocks.note: belonging to him, a man
Disraeli led the Conservative Party, whose members are Tories

explanation.surface: Archives belonging to the backers of the Victorian prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Disraeli was a Conservative prime minister of Britain, so his supporters were Tories.
explanation.definitionFit: Accounts of past events written down are chronicles of what happened, plural nouns like past records.

clue.text: Perhaps one whose life-style does him honour

definitions.text: Perhaps one whose life-style does him honour

blocks.clueFragment: Perhaps one whose life-style does him honour
blocks.note: surface reading: a man whose way of living earns him respect

blocks.clueFragment: Perhaps one whose life-style does him honour
blocks.note: setter's reading: a life member of the House of Lords, whose title or style is an honour

explanation.walkthrough: Life-style splits into life and style: a life ____ holds a non-hereditary title, and a style is the form of address a title gives, such as Lord.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the British nobility, including one given a title only for life, carries an honorific form of address.

clue.text: Month on a Roman road for Cleopatra's rival

indicators.note: in a down clue one thing on another sits above it, so the first part comes first

blocks.note: OCT is the calendar abbreviation for October
taken as written
via is Latin for road, as in the Via Appia

explanation.surface: A month spent travelling a Roman road to reach Cleopatra's enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Antony's Roman wife, sister of Octavian, competed with the Egyptian queen for his loyalty.

clue.text: A Burmese type of girl's name?

blocks.note: first meaning: a member of an ethnic people of Burma and Thailand
second meaning: a common female first name

explanation.surface: Asking whether a certain name is typically Burmese.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a hill people of eastern Burma and is also a popular given name for women.

clue.text: German alternative to border flower

blocks.note: first meaning: the German word for or
second meaning: a river, something that flows, forming the German-Polish frontier

explanation.surface: A German replacement for a plant in a garden border.
explanation.walkthrough: Flower is crossword shorthand for a river, read as flow-er; this one marks the boundary between Germany and Poland.
explanation.definitionFit: The German conjunction meaning or offers an alternative, and the same spelling names the river along Germany's eastern frontier.

clue.text: Poor little Edward's aunt not fully gratified

indicators.note: a word not fully present is cut short, losing its last letter
poor suggests something in bad shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: Ted is a pet form of Edward, with the possessive s
taken as written, before shortening

explanation.surface: Sympathy for a little boy's aunt, who never quite got satisfaction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not fully' does double duty, trimming aunt and negating gratified; old Times clues were looser than today's.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer means not satisfied, the negative of gratified once 'not' from the wordplay is read with it.

clue.text: Peacock attribute of mountain sheep

blocks.note: surface reading: a quality that a peacock shares with hill sheep
setter's reading: the quality the poet Thomas Love Peacock gave mountain sheep in his War Song of Dinas Vawr

explanation.walkthrough: Peacock is the novelist and poet: 'The mountain sheep are ____, But the valley sheep are fatter'. The comparative is quoted from that line.
explanation.definitionFit: In Peacock's verse the hill flock is called more pleasant-tasting than the valley flock, a comparative adjective.

clue.text: Pottery village of one-time BBC fame ?

definitions.text: Pottery village of one-time BBC fame

blocks.clueFragment: Pottery village of one-time BBC fame
blocks.note: surface reading: a ceramics-making village once featured on television

blocks.clueFragment: Pottery village of one-time BBC fame
blocks.note: setter's reading: the imaginary village belonging to comedian Gillie Potter, whose radio talks made it famous

explanation.walkthrough: Pottery here means of Potter: Gillie Potter's BBC radio monologues reported the doings of a fictional English village of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The comic's invented village, famed from his broadcasts in the 1930s and 1940s, is the hamlet the clue describes.

clue.text: The terrible start of a “ Scottish ” story

definitions.note: the answer is the name that the epithet the Terrible belongs to

indicators.note: only the opening part of the title is kept, the end being dropped

blocks.note: a novel by Sir Walter Scott, so a Scott-ish story

explanation.surface: A frightening opening to a Scottish tale.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks on Scottish hint at a pun: Scott-ish, by Walter Scott. His novel's first four letters give the tsar known as the Terrible.
explanation.definitionFit: The first Russian tsar is remembered with the epithet the Terrible, so that phrase points to his given name.

clue.text: Reckoning science to be additionally useful

blocks.clueFragment: Reckoning science to be additionally useful
blocks.note: surface reading: a calculating discipline that is also handy

blocks.clueFragment: Reckoning science to be additionally useful
blocks.note: setter's reading: the branch of mathematics that is useful for addition

explanation.walkthrough: Additionally sounds like 'as well', but it means by way of addition, one of the four basic operations of this branch of mathematics.
explanation.definitionFit: The branch of mathematics dealing with counting and calculation with numbers is the science of reckoning.

clue.text: Crazy telegram after the dance

indicators.note: after places the first-named part behind the second in the answer

blocks.note: a hay or hey is an old country dance
a wire is an informal word for a telegram

explanation.surface: An alarming telegram arriving after the party dance.
explanation.definitionFit: To go haywire means to go wildly wrong or out of control, so as an adjective it is crazy or erratic.

clue.text: Charged new rent to you Spanish

indicators.note: new means made over, so the letters following are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
usted is the polite Spanish word for you

explanation.surface: A Spanish tenant billed a higher rent by the landlord.
explanation.definitionFit: To be charged with a task or duty is to have it handed to you in trust, so the past participle matches.

clue.text: Encroachments on fashionable anchorages

blocks.note: in means currently popular
roads, or roadsteads, are sheltered waters where ships ride at anchor

explanation.surface: Raids on smart moorings where yachts lie at anchor.
explanation.walkthrough: Roads in the nautical sense is a stretch of sheltered water off a coast, as in Hampton Roads.
explanation.definitionFit: Making advances into territory or a market belonging to someone else is gradual intrusion, plural like encroachments.

clue.text: Minor occupations limiting scope for sport

blocks.note: first meaning: secondary jobs done alongside a main one
second meaning: the boundary markings along the edges of a pitch or court

explanation.surface: Second jobs that cut down on time for games.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both supplementary businesses held besides one's main work and the markings that bound a playing field.

clue.text: Lowest kind of nuisance on the river

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing on another follows it, so this part comes second

blocks.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and another in Wales and England
a pest is a type of nuisance

explanation.surface: The worst sort of pest found by the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lowest kind' looks like one phrase meaning the worst sort; the definition stops at Lowest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something furthest down, at the greatest depth, is the most profound, so the superlative means lowest.

clue.text: Passage taken out of a pamphlet?

blocks.note: ex is Latin for out of, as in ex officio
a tract is a short pamphlet, often religious or political

explanation.surface: A section quoted from a small booklet.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer, a piece lifted from a text.
explanation.definitionFit: A short section copied from a book or document is an excerpt or quoted piece of writing, a passage.

clue.text: How a theatre performer got things sewn up

definitions.text: How a theatre performer got things sewn up

blocks.clueFragment: How a theatre performer got things sewn up
blocks.note: surface reading: how an actor clinched a deal or a role

blocks.clueFragment: How a theatre performer got things sewn up
blocks.note: setter's reading: what a surgeon in the operating theatre did, stitching a wound closed

explanation.walkthrough: Theatre suggests the stage, but it is the operating theatre, and the performer is the surgeon who performs the operation.
explanation.definitionFit: To close a wound or incision with surgical stitches is the surgeon's way of sewing things up.

clue.text: Officialdom's rules for colour recording

blocks.note: red is a colour
a tape is a recording

explanation.surface: Bureaucratic regulations governing colour sound recordings.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive bureaucratic procedure, named after the ribbon once used to tie official papers, is the rules of officialdom.

clue.text: Out of breath and behind time

blocks.note: first meaning: dead, having breathed one's last, as in the deceased
second meaning: after the expected hour

explanation.surface: Someone panting because they are running behind schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: Out of breath suggests panting, but taken literally it means no longer breathing, as in 'the ____ king'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes someone recently deceased and also anything arriving after the proper time.

clue.text: Miss Ashton makes her name in opera

definitions.text: Miss Ashton makes her name in opera

blocks.clueFragment: Miss Ashton makes her name in opera
blocks.note: surface reading: a singer called Ashton becomes famous at the opera house

blocks.clueFragment: Miss Ashton makes her name in opera
blocks.note: setter's reading: what Scott's heroine Lucy Ashton is called in Donizetti's opera

explanation.walkthrough: Lucy Ashton is the heroine of Scott's The Bride of Lammermoor; in Donizetti's opera based on it her name takes its Italian form.
explanation.definitionFit: Donizetti's heroine of Lammermoor is the Italian rendering of Lucy, the name Scott gave Miss Ashton.

clue.text: Trifling award for MP involved with late duty

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters that follow are mixed together

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A token honour handed to a member of parliament for working late.
explanation.walkthrough: A putty medal is an old British jocular phrase for a worthless reward, one made of window putty rather than metal.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a mock decoration given for a trivial achievement, a worthless or trifling award.

clue.text: Give Uncle Toby's man a haircut

blocks.note: first meaning: Corporal ____, Uncle Toby's servant in Sterne's Tristram Shandy
second meaning: a light cut to tidy the hair

explanation.surface: Instructions to cut the hair of Uncle Toby's servant.
explanation.walkthrough: Uncle Toby is the gentle old soldier in Laurence Sterne's novel Tristram Shandy; his loyal servant is a corporal.
explanation.definitionFit: The corporal in Sterne's novel bears the name, and the same word is a noun for a light haircut.

clue.text: Found company to play with

blocks.note: first meaning: to found metal is to shape it in a mould
second meaning: the actors performing together in a play

explanation.surface: Someone discovered friends to play games with.
explanation.walkthrough: Found looks like the past of find; it is the verb to found, to pour molten metal into a mould.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal is shaped by pouring into a mould, and the term also names the full set of actors in a production.

clue.text: Classical French lover is vociferous

blocks.note: Cl is a dictionary abbreviation for classical
amant is the French word for a lover

explanation.surface: A lover from classical France who makes a lot of noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Insistently loud and demanding attention, an adjective synonym for clamorous or shouting, as in vociferous.

clue.text: Not yet finally dispatched by rail

blocks.note: first meaning: under way and still in progress, not yet finished
second meaning: travelling inside a railway carriage

explanation.surface: Goods awaiting dispatch on the railway.
explanation.walkthrough: Dispatched suggests posting a parcel, but here it means finished off; the phrase means set in motion and still going.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in progress, with business under way but unfinished, and literally riding aboard a railway carriage.

clue.text: “ O Attic shape! Fair - (Keats)

blocks.note: surface reading: a line of poetry with its last word missing
setter's reading: the gap is filled from Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn, which addresses the urn's painted figures

explanation.walkthrough: The full line in Keats's ode reads 'O Attic shape! Fair ____!', praising the posed figures painted on the Greek urn.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the noun Keats used for the graceful pose or posture of the figures on the urn.

clue.text: Prison officers' wages

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for jail warders
second meaning: old British slang for pay or salary

explanation.surface: The pay received by jail guards.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are British slang: a screw is a prison warder, and a screw is also a wage, as in earning a good screw.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang plural names jail guards and also weekly pay, so it fits both halves; the apostrophe is surface dressing.
